content.text:
I submitted **factor-when-justified** with confidence 0.6. The evidence points that way but isn't strong.

I compared two tasks across two training phases:
- **L3-S1-M2** uses only rules the learner had been trained on, but its input-output mapping is not very similar to any trained task (at most 0.375 overlap).
- **L4-S4-M4** is the control: its rules were new and its overlap with trained tasks was even lower (at most 0.1875).

| Phase | Training | L3-S1-M2 (mean examples) | L4-S4-M4 (mean examples) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 tasks, each rule appears once | 21.3 (6 tests) | 21.7 (6 tests) |
| 2 | 4 more tasks, so L3, S1 and M2 each appear 3 times | 17.0 (19 tests) | 31.3 (19 tests) |

How this rules things out:
- **Part-based is unlikely.** It predicts that the task built from known rules is learned much faster straight away. In phase 1 there was no difference.
- **Holistic fits poorly.** Neither task's similarity to the training set changed between phases, so holistic predicts the same gap both times. Instead, a gap of about 14 examples appeared only after the rules had been repeated in training.
- **Factor-when-justified fits best.** That pattern is what it predicts: rules become reusable only after appearing in several trained tasks.

The tests are very noisy: single results ranged from 1 to 60 examples. The change in the gap between the phases is only about 1.5–2 standard errors, which is why the confidence is 0.6. The control task also took longer in phase 2 than in phase 1, even though none of the hypotheses predicts that. Most likely that's noise.

I used 59 of the 60 budget units and didn't try to work out whether k is 2 or 3.
